courseDescr: Continuation of CHINLANG 2. Daily sections may be set at the beginning of the quarter to suit schedule requirements. Fulfills the University language requirement. Prerequisite: Placement Test, CHINLANG 2.
original_descr: Continuation of CHINLANG 2. Daily sections may be set at the beginning of the quarter to suit schedule requirements. Fulfills the University language requirement. Prerequisite: Placement Test, CHINLANG 2.
expanded_descr: First-Year Modern Chinese, Third Quarter is a continuation of CHINLANG 2, designed for students who have successfully completed the placement test and are currently enrolled in CHINLANG 2. This course builds on the foundational skills introduced in the first quarter, advancing students’ proficiency in speaking, listening, reading, and writing modern Chinese. Daily class sections are scheduled at the beginning of the quarter to accommodate students’ overall timetable requirements, ensuring flexibility while maintaining a consistent learning pace. Successful completion of this course satisfies the University’s language requirement, allowing students to meet the mandated foreign‑language component of their degree program. Prerequisite: Placement Test, CHINLANG 2.

courseDescr: One-year sequence designed to develop intermediate proficiency, with additional emphasis on functional applications and reading and writing standard Arabic. Prerequisite: Placement Test, ARABLANG 3.
original_descr: One-year sequence designed to develop intermediate proficiency, with additional emphasis on functional applications and reading and writing standard Arabic. Prerequisite: Placement Test, ARABLANG 3.
expanded_descr: This one‑year sequence is intended to guide students toward intermediate proficiency in Arabic, placing particular focus on functional language use as well as the development of reading and writing skills in standard Arabic. Throughout the course, learners will engage with authentic texts and practical communication tasks that reinforce both spoken and written competencies. The curriculum builds on foundational knowledge and prepares students for more advanced study by emphasizing real‑world applications of the language. Successful enrollment requires completion of the placement test and prior completion of ARABLANG 3, ensuring that all participants possess the necessary background to benefit fully from the material.

courseDescr: Completes second-year sequence in two rather than three quarters. For students with previous knowledge of Arabic. Prerequisite: Placement Test, ARABLANG 2A or 3.
original_descr: Completes second-year sequence in two rather than three quarters. For students with previous knowledge of Arabic. Prerequisite: Placement Test, ARABLANG 2A or 3.
expanded_descr: This accelerated offering completes the second‑year Arabic sequence in two quarters instead of the usual three, allowing students to progress more quickly while maintaining the same rigorous standards. It is designed specifically for learners who already possess a solid foundation in Arabic, as demonstrated by successful completion of the placement test and prior enrollment in either ARABLANG 2A or ARABLANG 3. By condensing the curriculum, the course provides an intensive, focused experience that builds on existing language skills and prepares students for advanced study. All prerequisites and restrictions remain unchanged, ensuring that only appropriately prepared students enroll.

courseDescr: Introduction to techniques, materials, and vocabulary in oil painting. Still life, landscape, and figure used as subject matter. Emphasis is on painting and drawing from life. (lower level)
original_descr: Introduction to techniques, materials, and vocabulary in oil painting. Still life, landscape, and figure used as subject matter. Emphasis is on painting and drawing from life. (lower level)
expanded_descr: This lower‑level course offers an introduction to the fundamental techniques, materials, and terminology essential for oil painting. Students will explore a range of subject matter, including still life arrangements, landscape scenes, and the human figure, while placing a strong emphasis on painting and drawing directly from life. Through guided practice, participants will become familiar with the properties of oil paints, appropriate brushwork, surface preparation, and the language used to discuss visual elements and compositional decisions. The class is designed to build a solid foundation in both the practical and conceptual aspects of oil painting, preparing students for further study in the medium.

courseDescr: Practicum. Students develop independent research projects and write research proposals. How to formulate a research question; how to integrate theory and field site; and step-by-step proposal writing.
original_descr: Practicum. Students develop independent research projects and write research proposals. How to formulate a research question; how to integrate theory and field site; and step-by-step proposal writing.
expanded_descr: This practicum provides students with hands‑on experience in developing independent research projects and crafting formal research proposals. Participants will learn how to formulate a clear, focused research question and how to integrate relevant theoretical frameworks with the specifics of a chosen field site. The workshop guides students through each stage of the proposal‑writing process, offering step‑by‑step instruction on structuring the document, articulating objectives, and presenting methodology. By the end of the course, students will have produced a complete draft proposal that reflects a coherent research plan, demonstrating their ability to connect theory to practice and to communicate scholarly ideas effectively.

courseDescr: Continuation of CHINLANG 1.  Daily sections may be set at the beginning of the quarter to suit schedule requirements.Prerequisite: placement test, CHINLANG 1.
original_descr: Continuation of CHINLANG 1.  Daily sections may be set at the beginning of the quarter to suit schedule requirements.Prerequisite: placement test, CHINLANG 1.
expanded_descr: This course is the second‑quarter continuation of CHINLANG 1, designed for students who have successfully completed the introductory level and passed the required placement test. It builds on the foundational skills developed in CHINLANG 1, offering further practice in listening, speaking, reading, and writing modern Chinese. Daily class sections will be scheduled at the start of the quarter to accommodate students’ overall timetables and to meet institutional scheduling requirements. Enrollment is limited to those who have satisfied the prerequisite placement test and have earned a passing grade in CHINLANG 1, ensuring that all participants possess the necessary background for continued language development.

courseDescr: Techniques such as monotype, monoprint, photocopy transfers, linocut and woodcut, intaglio etching. Demonstrations of these techniques. Field trips to local print collections or print exhibitions. (lower level)
original_descr: Techniques such as monotype, monoprint, photocopy transfers, linocut and woodcut, intaglio etching. Demonstrations of these techniques. Field trips to local print collections or print exhibitions. (lower level)
expanded_descr: This lower‑level course offers an introductory survey of printmaking, focusing on hands‑on exploration of several foundational techniques. Students will work with monotype and monoprint processes, experiment with photocopy transfers, and develop skills in relief methods such as linocut and woodcut. The curriculum also includes instruction in intaglio etching, providing a balanced view of both additive and subtractive printmaking approaches. Throughout the term, the instructor will provide live demonstrations of each technique, allowing students to observe professional methods before applying them in studio practice. Complementary field trips to local print collections or print exhibitions further contextualize the work, exposing students to historical and contemporary examples of the medium.

courseDescr: Completes Second-year sequence in two rather than three quarters. For students with previous knowledge of Arabic. Prerequisite: Placement Test, ARABLANG 21A.
original_descr: Completes Second-year sequence in two rather than three quarters. For students with previous knowledge of Arabic. Prerequisite: Placement Test, ARABLANG 21A.
expanded_descr: This accelerated offering completes the second‑year Arabic sequence in just two quarters instead of the usual three, providing a faster path for students who already possess a solid foundation in the language. It is designed specifically for learners with prior Arabic experience and who are ready to engage in an intensive, continuous study schedule. Enrollment is limited to those who have successfully passed the department’s placement test and who have satisfied the prerequisite requirement of ARABLANG 21A. By maintaining the same rigorous curriculum in a condensed timeframe, the course enables qualified students to advance their proficiency efficiently while meeting the established academic standards.

courseDescr: Continuation of CHINLANG 3. Listening, speaking, reading, writing. Daily sections may be set at the beginning of the quarter to suit schedule requirements. Prerequisite: Placement Test, CHINLANG 3.
original_descr: Continuation of CHINLANG 3. Listening, speaking, reading, writing. Daily sections may be set at the beginning of the quarter to suit schedule requirements. Prerequisite: Placement Test, CHINLANG 3.
expanded_descr: This course is the second‑year continuation of CHINLANG 3, focusing on the development of listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills in modern Chinese. Students will build on the foundation established in the prerequisite CHINLANG 3 and will be expected to demonstrate proficiency as confirmed by a placement test. Throughout the quarter, daily language sections will be scheduled at the beginning of the term in order to accommodate the specific schedule requirements of the program. The class emphasizes integrated practice across all four language domains, reinforcing vocabulary, grammar, and cultural nuances while preparing students for more advanced Chinese language study.

courseDescr: No knowledge of Greek is assumed. Vocabulary and syntax of the classical language.
original_descr: No knowledge of Greek is assumed. Vocabulary and syntax of the classical language.
expanded_descr: This introductory course assumes no prior knowledge of Greek; it is designed for complete beginners. Students will encounter the fundamental elements of the classical language, focusing on building a basic vocabulary and understanding essential syntactic structures. Through systematic exposure to core lexical items and grammatical patterns, participants will develop the ability to recognize and construct simple sentences. The curriculum emphasizes the acquisition of foundational linguistic tools necessary for further study of ancient Greek texts, ensuring that all learners start with a solid grounding in both word meanings and the rules that govern their arrangement. No prerequisites are required, and no additional restrictions apply.

courseTitle: Third-Year Modern Chinese for Bilingual Students, First Quarter
courseDescr: Continuation of CHINLANG 23B. Equivalent to CHINLANG 101. For students with advanced listening and speaking abilities, but lacking equivalent knowledge in reading and writing.  Prerequisite: Placement Test, CHINLANG 23B.
course_title: Third-Year Modern Chinese for Bilingual Students, First Quarter
original_descr: Continuation of CHINLANG 23B. Equivalent to CHINLANG 101. For students with advanced listening and speaking abilities, but lacking equivalent knowledge in reading and writing.  Prerequisite: Placement Test, CHINLANG 23B.
expanded_descr: This course is the next step in the sequence after CHINLANG 23B and is considered equivalent to CHINLANG 101. It is designed specifically for bilingual students who already possess advanced listening and speaking skills in Mandarin Chinese but who have not yet developed comparable proficiency in reading and writing. The class will focus on building literacy foundations, introducing Chinese characters, basic grammar structures, and reading comprehension strategies while continuing to reinforce oral communication. Students must have successfully completed the placement test and be enrolled in CHINLANG 23B before registering for this quarter’s offering.

courseDescr: Intensive review of Latin syntax and introduction to prose composition.
original_descr: Intensive review of Latin syntax and introduction to prose composition.
expanded_descr: This course offers an intensive review of Latin syntax, providing students with a focused and thorough reinforcement of grammatical structures, declensions, and conjugations essential to reading and interpreting Latin texts. Building on that foundation, the class introduces the basics of prose composition in Latin, guiding learners through the process of constructing clear, coherent sentences and short passages. Emphasis is placed on applying syntactic rules to produce original Latin prose, while reinforcing analytical skills developed through the review component. The curriculum balances rigorous syntactic practice with practical composition exercises, ensuring participants gain confidence in both understanding and creating Latin language material.

courseTitle: Undergraduate Directed Reading in Comparative Medicine
courseDescr: May be taken as a prelude to research and may also involve participation in a lab or research group seminar and/or library research.
course_title: Undergraduate Directed Reading in Comparative Medicine
original_descr: May be taken as a prelude to research and may also involve participation in a lab or research group seminar and/or library research.
expanded_descr: This undergraduate directed reading course in Comparative Medicine is designed to serve as a formal prelude to independent research activities. Students enroll with the expectation that the experience will help them transition smoothly into laboratory work or scholarly projects. The structure of the course may include active participation in a research laboratory, attendance at a research‑group seminar, and/or focused library research, depending on the specific arrangement agreed upon with the supervising faculty member. By engaging in these components, students gain exposure to the methods and literature of comparative medicine, preparing them for more advanced investigative work while adhering to the course’s established prerequisites and restrictions.

courseDescr: Repeatable once for units. Prerequisite: CHINLANG 23.
original_descr: Repeatable once for units. Prerequisite: CHINLANG 23.
expanded_descr: This course offers a focused, interactive environment for students who have successfully completed CHINLANG 23 and wish to deepen their spoken Chinese abilities. Designed for the first quarter, it emphasizes fluid, natural conversation through a variety of authentic topics, encouraging participants to practice pronunciation, idiomatic expressions, and cultural nuances in real‑time dialogue. Class activities include role‑plays, discussions, and collaborative exercises that build confidence and fluency while reinforcing previously learned grammar and vocabulary. The offering is repeatable one additional time for credit, allowing students to further refine their conversational skills and achieve greater proficiency before advancing to higher‑level language study.

courseDescr: World history from the origins of humanity to the Black Death. Focuses on the evolution of complex societies, wealth, violence, hierarchy, and large-scale belief systems.
original_descr: World history from the origins of humanity to the Black Death. Focuses on the evolution of complex societies, wealth, violence, hierarchy, and large-scale belief systems.
expanded_descr: This course offers a sweeping survey of world history, beginning with the earliest emergence of Homo sapiens and extending through the transformative period of the Black Death. Students will examine how primitive groups gave rise to increasingly complex societies, tracing the development of economic systems, patterns of wealth accumulation, and the mechanisms of violence that shaped intergroup relations. The curriculum also investigates the formation and maintenance of hierarchical structures, exploring how power was organized and exercised across different cultures. In addition, the course analyzes the evolution of large‑scale belief systems, considering their role in uniting populations, legitimizing authority, and influencing social change throughout the ages.

courseTitle: Reporting, Writing, and Understanding the News
courseDescr: Techniques of news reporting and writing. The value and role of news in democratic societies. Gateway class to journalism. Prerequisite for many COMM 177/277 classes.
course_title: Reporting, Writing, and Understanding the News
original_descr: Techniques of news reporting and writing. The value and role of news in democratic societies. Gateway class to journalism. Prerequisite for many COMM 177/277 classes.
expanded_descr: This course introduces students to the fundamental techniques of news reporting and writing, emphasizing the practical skills needed to gather, verify, and present information clearly and accurately. It also examines the value and role of news within democratic societies, exploring how journalism contributes to informed citizenship, public discourse, and accountability. Designed as a gateway class to journalism, the curriculum provides a solid foundation for further study and prepares students for advanced coursework. Successful completion of this course satisfies the prerequisite requirement for many COMM 177/277 classes, ensuring that students are equipped with the essential background before progressing to more specialized communication and media studies.

courseTitle: Additional Topics in Teaching Computer Science
courseDescr: Students build on the teaching skills developed in CS198. Focus is on techniques used to teach topics covered in CS106B. Prerequisite: successful completion of CS198.
course_title: Additional Topics in Teaching Computer Science
original_descr: Students build on the teaching skills developed in CS198. Focus is on techniques used to teach topics covered in CS106B. Prerequisite: successful completion of CS198.
expanded_descr: Students expand upon the foundational teaching abilities they cultivated in CS198, deepening their pedagogical repertoire through targeted practice. The course concentrates specifically on instructional techniques and strategies that are effective for conveying the material presented in CS106B, allowing participants to refine how they explain algorithms, data structures, and related concepts. By building directly on the experience gained in the prerequisite course, students will engage in activities that enhance their capacity to design lessons, manage classroom dynamics, and assess student understanding within the context of CS106B topics. Prerequisite: successful completion of CS198.

courseDescr: Explores operating system concepts including concurrency, synchronization, scheduling, processes, virtual memory, I/O, file systems, and protection. Available as a substitute for CS110 that fulfills any requirement satisfied by CS110.
original_descr: Explores operating system concepts including concurrency, synchronization, scheduling, processes, virtual memory, I/O, file systems, and protection. Available as a substitute for CS110 that fulfills any requirement satisfied by CS110.
expanded_descr: This course provides an in‑depth examination of core operating system concepts. Topics include the fundamentals of concurrency and the mechanisms used to achieve synchronization among processes, as well as the principles behind scheduling algorithms that allocate CPU time. Students will study the structure and management of processes, explore virtual memory techniques, and investigate input/output strategies. The curriculum also covers the organization and operation of file systems and the methods used to enforce system protection and security. The class may be taken as a substitute for CS110 and satisfies any academic requirement that CS110 fulfills.

courseDescr: Historical and contemporary as a broad genre including travel and nature writing, memoir, biography, journalism, and the personal essay. Students use creative means to express factual content.
original_descr: Historical and contemporary as a broad genre including travel and nature writing, memoir, biography, journalism, and the personal essay. Students use creative means to express factual content.
expanded_descr: This course examines Creative Nonfiction as a broad literary genre that encompasses both historical and contemporary works. It includes travel writing, nature writing, memoir, biography, journalism, and the personal essay, exploring how each form blends factual content with artistic expression. Students will study representative texts from each sub‑genre, analyzing the techniques writers use to convey truth while employing narrative strategies, vivid description, and personal voice. Through reading, discussion, and writing assignments, participants will learn to apply creative methods to their own factual material, developing work that is both accurate and compelling without sacrificing the integrity of the underlying facts.

courseDescr: For Alternative Spring Break program leaders. The skills and philosophical framework to develop and lead an ASB experience. May be repeat for credit
original_descr: For Alternative Spring Break program leaders. The skills and philosophical framework to develop and lead an ASB experience. May be repeat for credit
expanded_descr: This course is designed specifically for leaders of Alternative Spring Break (ASB) programs. It offers a comprehensive exploration of the essential skills and underlying philosophical framework needed to design, organize, and effectively lead an ASB experience. Participants will engage with the core concepts that inform service‑learning practice, examine strategies for community partnership, and refine the leadership techniques that support meaningful student involvement. The curriculum emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical application, ensuring that each leader is prepared to create impactful, reflective, and ethically grounded service experiences. The course may be repeated for credit, allowing continued development and mastery of ASB leadership competencies.

courseDescr: Issues of poetic craft. How elements of form, music, structure, and content work together to create meaning and experience in a poem.
original_descr: Issues of poetic craft. How elements of form, music, structure, and content work together to create meaning and experience in a poem.
expanded_descr: This course explores the essential issues of poetic craft, examining how the various elements of form, music, structure, and content interact to generate meaning and shape the reader’s experience within a poem. Students will investigate the ways in which formal choices—such as meter, rhyme, line length, and stanzaic patterns—combine with musical qualities like rhythm, sound, and cadence to produce a cohesive artistic effect. The class also considers how structural decisions and thematic content reinforce one another, creating layers of significance that deepen emotional resonance and intellectual engagement. Through close reading and analysis, participants develop a nuanced understanding of how these components work together to construct powerful, memorable poetry.

courseDescr: Graduates enroll in PHIL274.
original_descr: Graduates enroll in PHIL274.
expanded_descr: This upper‑level offering, Ethics Beyond Consequences, serves as a capstone for students who have completed the required philosophy sequence. Upon successful completion, graduates automatically enroll in PHIL274, the designated advanced seminar that continues the exploration of moral theory. The course deepens analytical skills by examining ethical frameworks that extend beyond simple outcome‑based reasoning, encouraging rigorous debate and critical reflection. It builds directly on prior coursework, ensuring that participants are prepared for the transition to PHIL274 without any additional prerequisites or special conditions. Enrollment in PHIL274 is guaranteed for all who meet the graduation criteria for this class.

courseDescr: Continuation of FRENLANG 1. Proficiency-based. Development of discourse appropriate in French and Francophone contexts. Recent placement Test, completion of FRENLANG 1 or consent of French coordinator.
original_descr: Continuation of FRENLANG 1. Proficiency-based. Development of discourse appropriate in French and Francophone contexts. Recent placement Test, completion of FRENLANG 1 or consent of French coordinator.
expanded_descr: This course is the second‑quarter continuation of FRENLANG 1 and is offered to students who have demonstrated sufficient proficiency through a recent placement test, have successfully completed FRENLANG 1, or have obtained explicit consent from the French program coordinator.  It remains a proficiency‑based class, emphasizing the development of spoken and written discourse that is appropriate for a variety of French and Francophone contexts.  Students will build on foundational language skills, focusing on expanding vocabulary, refining grammatical accuracy, and practicing authentic communication situations.  The curriculum is designed to deepen cultural awareness while strengthening the ability to produce coherent, context‑sensitive French language output.

courseDescr: Proficiency-based. Development of discourse appropriate in French and Francophone contexts. Prerequisite: no previous exposure to French
original_descr: Proficiency-based. Development of discourse appropriate in French and Francophone contexts. Prerequisite: no previous exposure to French
expanded_descr: This first‑quarter, first‑year French course is designed as a proficiency‑based experience that introduces students to the fundamentals of communicating in French. Emphasis is placed on developing discourse that is appropriate for a variety of Francophone contexts, enabling learners to engage in everyday conversations, understand cultural nuances, and produce written and spoken language that reflects authentic usage. Through interactive activities, listening and reading exercises, and guided practice, students will build a solid foundation for future language study. No prior exposure to French is required; the prerequisite is simply that students have not previously studied the language.

courseDescr: Continuation of GERLANG1. Further development of socially and culturally appropriate proficiency in interpersonal, interpretive, and presentational spheres.Prerequisite: Placement, GERLANG1.
original_descr: Continuation of GERLANG1. Further development of socially and culturally appropriate proficiency in interpersonal, interpretive, and presentational spheres.Prerequisite: Placement, GERLANG1.
expanded_descr: This course builds directly on the material covered in GERLANG1, serving as the second‑quarter continuation for first‑year students. It deepens learners’ ability to communicate in German across interpersonal, interpretive, and presentational contexts, emphasizing socially and culturally appropriate language use. Students will refine speaking, listening, reading, and writing skills while gaining greater confidence in real‑world interactions and cultural nuances. The curriculum expands on previously introduced vocabulary, grammar structures, and communicative strategies, encouraging more sophisticated expression and comprehension. Successful enrollment requires completion of the placement assessment and prior completion of GERLANG1, ensuring that all participants share the necessary foundational proficiency.

courseDescr: First-quarter of three-quarter First-Year Gerlang sequence. Emphasis is on developing beginning proficiency in interpersonal, interpretive, and presentational spheres.Prerequisite:  no experience with German or Placement.
original_descr: First-quarter of three-quarter First-Year Gerlang sequence. Emphasis is on developing beginning proficiency in interpersonal, interpretive, and presentational spheres.Prerequisite:  no experience with German or Placement.
expanded_descr: This course constitutes the first quarter of a three‑quarter introductory sequence in German. It is designed for students who have no prior experience with the language and who have not completed any placement testing. The emphasis throughout the quarter is on building beginning proficiency across the three communicative domains: interpersonal interaction, interpretive comprehension, and presentational expression. Students will engage in activities that develop basic listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills, laying a solid foundation for continued study in the subsequent quarters of the First‑Year German series. No prerequisite knowledge or placement is required to enroll.

courseDescr: Continuation of ITALLANG 2A or Italian 3. For students going to Florence. Completes second-year sequence in two rather than three quarters. Prerequisite: placement test, ITALLANG 2A, ITALLANG 3.
original_descr: Continuation of ITALLANG 2A or Italian 3. For students going to Florence. Completes second-year sequence in two rather than three quarters. Prerequisite: placement test, ITALLANG 2A, ITALLANG 3.
expanded_descr: This accelerated offering serves as the continuation of either ITALLANG 2A or Italian 3 and is designed specifically for students who will be traveling to Florence. It enables participants to complete the second‑year Italian language sequence in two quarters instead of the usual three, allowing a more rapid progression while maintaining the same rigorous standards. Enrollment is contingent upon meeting the prerequisite requirements, which include a satisfactory placement test result and successful completion of ITALLANG 2A and ITALLANG 3. The course therefore provides a focused, intensive experience that fulfills the second‑year curriculum within a compressed timeframe for eligible students.

courseDescr: Class is closed by design.  Please contact instructor Erika Arul (mailto:earul@stanford.edu) for permission to enroll. Preference to Music majors and minors.
original_descr: Class is closed by design.  Please contact instructor Erika Arul (mailto:earul@stanford.edu) for permission to enroll. Preference to Music majors and minors.
expanded_descr: This course is intentionally closed to the general student body; enrollment is limited by design. Prospective students must obtain explicit permission from the instructor, Erika Arul (email: earul@stanford.edu), before they may register. The instructor will consider requests and grant access at her discretion. Preference for admission will be given to those who are declared Music majors or minors, reflecting the program’s focus on developing foundational aural skills within the discipline. Applicants who do not meet the Music major or minor criteria may still inquire, but they should be aware that priority will be accorded to eligible Music students.

courseDescr: Techniques for organizing data, computing, and interpreting measures of central tendency, variability, and association. Estimation, confidence intervals, tests of hypotheses, correlation, and regression.
original_descr: Techniques for organizing data, computing, and interpreting measures of central tendency, variability, and association. Estimation, confidence intervals, tests of hypotheses, correlation, and regression.
expanded_descr: This course introduces fundamental statistical techniques for organizing and summarizing data, emphasizing the calculation and interpretation of measures of central tendency such as the mean, median, and mode, as well as measures of variability including range, variance, and standard deviation. Students will explore methods for assessing association between variables, learning to compute and interpret correlation coefficients and to construct simple linear regression models. The curriculum also covers basic inferential concepts, including point estimation, the construction and meaning of confidence intervals, and the formulation and testing of statistical hypotheses. Throughout, emphasis is placed on developing clear, quantitative reasoning skills for analyzing real‑world data sets.

courseDescr: A beginning Russian course. Proficiency based communicative approach. Introduction to essential vocabulary and grammar, Russian culture and the Russian view of reality.
original_descr: A beginning Russian course. Proficiency based communicative approach. Introduction to essential vocabulary and grammar, Russian culture and the Russian view of reality.
expanded_descr: This introductory Russian language class is designed for first‑year students during the first quarter. It follows a proficiency‑based, communicative approach that emphasizes speaking, listening, reading, and writing skills from the very start. Students will be introduced to essential vocabulary and fundamental grammar structures that form the basis for everyday conversation. In addition to language fundamentals, the course offers a survey of Russian culture, exploring traditions, customs, and artistic expressions, as well as an examination of the Russian perspective on reality and worldview. The curriculum balances linguistic practice with cultural insight, providing a solid foundation for continued study of Russian.

courseTitle: First-Year Japanese Language, Culture, and Communication, First Quarter
courseDescr: First-year sequence enables students to converse, write, and read essays on topics such as personal history, experiences, familiar people.  72 kanji characters will be taught.
course_title: First-Year Japanese Language, Culture, and Communication, First Quarter
original_descr: First-year sequence enables students to converse, write, and read essays on topics such as personal history, experiences, familiar people.  72 kanji characters will be taught.
expanded_descr: The first‑year Japanese Language, Culture, and Communication course for the first quarter introduces students to foundational communication skills in Japanese. Throughout the term, learners will develop the ability to converse fluently on everyday subjects, compose written pieces, and read short essays that explore personal history, individual experiences, and familiar people. Instruction emphasizes practical usage of the language in authentic contexts, allowing students to express themselves confidently in both spoken and written forms. As part of the curriculum, a total of seventy‑two kanji characters will be taught, providing essential vocabulary for reading and writing tasks. This course lays the groundwork for continued study of Japanese language and culture.

courseDescr: Pre- or corequisite: 21.
original_descr: Pre- or corequisite: 21.
expanded_descr: Enrollment in Music History to 1600 is contingent upon satisfying a specific academic requirement: students must either have successfully completed, or be concurrently registered in, course number 21. This prerequisite—or corequisite—ensures that all participants possess the foundational knowledge deemed essential for engaging with the material presented in this survey of early music. Accordingly, prospective registrants should verify their academic record to confirm that they meet this condition before adding the class to their schedule. Failure to satisfy the pre‑ or corequisite stipulation will preclude enrollment, as the department strictly enforces this prerequisite to maintain curricular integrity.

courseDescr: Continuation of SWAHLANG 2. Prerequisite: SWAHLANG 2. Fulfills the University foreign language requirement.
original_descr: Continuation of SWAHLANG 2. Prerequisite: SWAHLANG 2. Fulfills the University foreign language requirement.
expanded_descr: This course is the third‑quarter offering of First‑Year Swahili and serves as a direct continuation of SWAHLANG 2. Students enrolling must have successfully completed SWAHLANG 2, as it is the stated prerequisite for continued study. The class builds on the foundational skills and vocabulary introduced in the prior semester, providing additional practice in speaking, listening, reading, and writing in Swahili. By participating in this course, students further develop their proficiency and cultural understanding of the language. Completion of First‑Year Swahili, Third Quarter satisfies the University’s foreign language requirement, contributing toward the broader curriculum goals for language competency.

courseDescr: This is the first year first quarter course in a three quarter sequence. Grammatical structures, vocabulary, and sentence patterns through speaking, reading, writing, and listening. Ukrainian culture.
original_descr: This is the first year first quarter course in a three quarter sequence. Grammatical structures, vocabulary, and sentence patterns through speaking, reading, writing, and listening. Ukrainian culture.
expanded_descr: This is the first‑year, first‑quarter course in a three‑quarter sequence designed for beginners.  The class introduces fundamental grammatical structures, essential vocabulary, and basic sentence patterns, and it provides extensive practice in speaking, reading, writing, and listening.  Students will engage with authentic Ukrainian texts and audio materials while developing the ability to construct simple utterances and comprehend everyday language.  Throughout the quarter, the curriculum integrates cultural content, offering insight into Ukrainian traditions, customs, and contemporary life.  By the end of the term, learners will have a solid foundation in the language’s core components and an appreciation for the cultural context in which Ukrainian is used.

courseDescr: Students undertake investigations sponsored by individual faculty members. Prerequisite: consent of instructor.
original_descr: Students undertake investigations sponsored by individual faculty members. Prerequisite: consent of instructor.
expanded_descr: Students engage in independent investigations that are directly sponsored by individual faculty members, allowing them to apply classroom learning to authentic scholarly work. Under the guidance of the sponsoring professor, each participant designs and conducts a research project, gathers and analyzes data, and contributes to the development of new knowledge within the discipline. The experience emphasizes critical thinking, methodological rigor, and scholarly communication, preparing students for advanced study or professional practice. Successful enrollment requires obtaining the explicit consent of the instructor who will supervise the project, ensuring that the student’s interests and the faculty member’s expertise are appropriately aligned.

courseDescr: Continuation of YDDSHLNG 3. Prerequisite: YDDSHLNG 3.
original_descr: Continuation of YDDSHLNG 3. Prerequisite: YDDSHLNG 3.
expanded_descr: This course is the second‑year continuation of the Yiddish language sequence, specifically the first quarter of the second‑year segment. It builds directly on the material covered in YDDSHLNG 3, reinforcing and extending the linguistic skills, vocabulary, and cultural understanding introduced previously. Students will engage in further practice of reading, writing, speaking, and listening in Yiddish, deepening their proficiency through structured classroom activities, assignments, and discussions that assume mastery of the foundational concepts from the prerequisite. Prerequisite: YDDSHLNG 3.

courseDescr: Current research topics in lasers, quantum electronics, optics, and photonics by faculty, students, and invited outside speakers. May be repeated for credit.
original_descr: Current research topics in lasers, quantum electronics, optics, and photonics by faculty, students, and invited outside speakers. May be repeated for credit.
expanded_descr: This seminar explores current research topics in lasers, quantum electronics, optics, and photonics, featuring presentations by faculty members, graduate and undergraduate students, and invited speakers from outside the university. Each session highlights recent advances and ongoing investigations in these fields, offering participants insight into cutting‑edge developments and the opportunity to engage with presenters through questions and discussion. The course is designed to complement existing curricula by providing a forum for scholarly exchange and interdisciplinary collaboration. Students may enroll in the seminar multiple times, receiving credit for each successful repetition, provided they meet any departmental registration requirements.

courseDescr: Quantum mechanics with examples related to spectroscopy. Includes time dependent perturbation theory, matrix formalism, density matrix formalism and angular momentum.  Prerequisite: CHEM 271 or equivalent quantum mechanics course.

courseTitle: Hip Hop I: Introduction to Hip Hop

courseDescr: Interdisciplinary approaches to understanding human-environment interactions with a focus on economics, policy, culture, history, and the role of the state.

courseDescr: Geometry of curves and surfaces in three-space. Parallel transport, curvature, and geodesics. Surfaces with constant curvature. Minimal surfaces. Prerequisite: Math 52.

Additional topics include the formulation and solution of recurrence relations, the development and manipulation of generating functions, and an introduction to basic asymptotic analysis. The material provides a solid foundation for further study and application of combinatorial methods.

Throughout the term, the focus remains on rigorous development of these topics and their interrelations. Prerequisite: Math 115 or 171.

courseTitle: Advanced Structural Concrete Behavior and Design

course_title: Advanced Structural Concrete Behavior and Design
original_descr: Behavior and design of reinforced and prestressed concrete for building and bridge design.  Topics will include  flexural behavior, prestressed concrete design, and two-way slab design & analysis, among others.
expanded_descr: This course examines the behavior and design of reinforced and prestressed concrete as applied to both building and bridge projects. The curriculum integrates theoretical concepts with practical design considerations, enabling participants to evaluate and optimize concrete elements for safety, serviceability, and durability. By the end of the course, learners will possess a comprehensive grasp of advanced concrete behavior and the associated design methodologies.

courseTitle: Exploring Advanced Chemical Research at Stanford

This presentation serves as an essential orientation to the department’s active research landscape.

courseDescr: Topics in the theory and empirics of economic growth. For PhD-level students.

Participants will engage with scholarly literature, discuss methodological challenges, and develop a nuanced understanding of how growth theory informs real‑world economic analysis.

courseDescr: Required for first-year ICME Ph.D. students; recommended for first-year ICME M.S. students interested in research. Presentations about research by Stanford faculty and researchers. May be repeated for credit.
original_descr: Required for first-year ICME Ph.D. students; recommended for first-year ICME M.S. students interested in research. Presentations about research by Stanford faculty and researchers. May be repeated for credit.

The course may be taken more than once for credit, allowing students to revisit the material and deepen their exposure to the institute’s research environment.

courseDescr: COMM PhD faculty talk about the department and its various research projects work.
original_descr: COMM PhD faculty talk about the department and its various research projects work.

By the end of the meeting, attendees will have a clearer understanding of the department’s academic profile and the diverse research work being pursued by its scholars.

courseDescr: Approaches to teaching English in the secondary school, including goals for instruction, teaching techniques, and methods of evaluation. STEP secondary only.

courseDescr: The purposes and programs of mathematics in the secondary curriculum; teaching materials, methods. Prerequisite: STEP student or consent of instructor. (STEP) 263A. Sum, 263B. Aut, 263C. Win
original_descr: The purposes and programs of mathematics in the secondary curriculum; teaching materials, methods. Prerequisite: STEP student or consent of instructor. (STEP) 263A. Sum, 263B. Aut, 263C. Win

courseDescr: This project-based lab course introduces students to the use of several maker tools for personal and academic projects.
original_descr: This project-based lab course introduces students to the use of several maker tools for personal and academic projects.

By the end of the term, students will have a solid foundation in the operation of several maker tools, preparing them to integrate these resources into future coursework, research, or independent endeavors.

courseDescr: Restricted to Economics Ph.D. students. Students present current research. May be repeated for credit.

The seminar emphasizes rigorous academic discourse and the development of presentation skills essential for conference and dissertation defense settings. Attendance and active participation are required, and the course may be repeated for additional credit, allowing students to refine their work and incorporate new data as their dissertations progress.

courseDescr: Analysis of quantitative and longitudinal data on national educational systems and political structures. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: consent of instructor.
original_descr: Analysis of quantitative and longitudinal data on national educational systems and political structures. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: consent of instructor.

The course is designed for repeated enrollment, allowing students to earn credit each time they successfully complete the required work. Enrollment is contingent upon obtaining the explicit consent of the instructor, which serves as the sole prerequisite for participation.

courseDescr: Dynamic and transient effects in lasers including spiking, Q-switching, mode locking, frequency modulation, frequency and spatial mode competition, linear and nonlinear pulse propagation, pulse shaping.  Formerly EE 232.
original_descr: Dynamic and transient effects in lasers including spiking, Q-switching, mode locking, frequency modulation, frequency and spatial mode competition, linear and nonlinear pulse propagation, pulse shaping.  Formerly EE 232.
expanded_descr: This course examines the dynamic and transient phenomena that occur in laser systems. Topics include the mechanisms and characteristics of spiking, Q‑switching, and mode‑locking, as well as techniques for frequency modulation. The curriculum also covers linear and nonlinear pulse propagation, providing insight into how pulses evolve as they travel through various media. In addition, the course addresses pulse shaping methods used to tailor temporal and spectral properties of laser output. Formerly listed as EE 232, the class retains its focus on fundamental laser dynamics and advanced modulation concepts.

courseTitle: Introduction to Graduate Study for Ph.D. Students

courseDescr: Weekly forum for ongoing epidemiologic research by faculty, staff, guests, and students, emphasizing research issues relevant to disease causation, prevention, and treatment. May be repeated for credit.
original_descr: Weekly forum for ongoing epidemiologic research by faculty, staff, guests, and students, emphasizing research issues relevant to disease causation, prevention, and treatment. May be repeated for credit.

courseDescr: Strategies and conventions for graduate writing. Emphasis is placed on fluency, organization, documentation, and appropriateness for writing tasks required in coursework.  May be repeated once for credit.

The emphasis on fluency helps learners write more smoothly and confidently, while the focus on organization ensures logical structure and coherence. Attention to documentation teaches correct citation practices, and the exploration of task‑specific appropriateness prepares students to adapt their writing to different academic assignments. courseTitle: Graduate Research Seminar in Jewish History

courseTitle: Professional Seminar for First-Year Ph.D. Graduate Students

course_title: Professional Seminar for First-Year Ph.D. Graduate Students

Participation is limited to those who have entered the Ph.D. program in their initial year, ensuring a shared academic foundation among all attendees.

courseDescr: Required of first- to third-year graduate students. Graduate students present and discuss recent papers in the literature. May be repeated for credit.
original_descr: Required of first- to third-year graduate students. Graduate students present and discuss recent papers in the literature. May be repeated for credit.

Participation is mandatory for eligible students, and the experience is intended to develop scholarly communication and analytical skills. The course may be repeated for additional credit, allowing students to deepen their exposure to current immunological research.

courseDescr: Enrollment limited to Ph.D., M.D./Ph.D., and medical students whose scholarly concentrations are in Immunology. Current research topics.
original_descr: Enrollment limited to Ph.D., M.D./Ph.D., and medical students whose scholarly concentrations are in Immunology. Current research topics.

By limiting attendance to students with a dedicated immunology focus, the seminar ensures that discussions remain highly relevant and advanced, supporting deep scholarly interaction among peers actively involved in immunological research.

courseDescr: Each week, we will cover a topic of interest to geoscientists by reading and discussing papers related to the dynamic interaction of life and landscape. Graduate students only.
original_descr: Each week, we will cover a topic of interest to geoscientists by reading and discussing papers related to the dynamic interaction of life and landscape. Graduate students only.

The course is designed exclusively for graduate students, fostering an advanced academic environment where emerging scholars can deepen their understanding of biogeomorphic systems. Through regular, structured sessions, students will develop the ability to evaluate scientific literature, articulate complex concepts, and contribute thoughtfully to ongoing conversations in the field.

courseDescr: Advanced sociolinguistic data collection techniques and data management methods applied to the study of a neighborhood in San Francisco. Topics do not include ethnographic methods. Field assignments required.
original_descr: Advanced sociolinguistic data collection techniques and data management methods applied to the study of a neighborhood in San Francisco. Topics do not include ethnographic methods. Field assignments required.

The curriculum emphasizes methodological rigor while deliberately excluding ethnographic methods, ensuring a focused approach to sociolinguistic inquiry. Through hands‑on practice, participants will refine their ability to design and implement fieldwork protocols, manage complex data sets, and produce reliable findings that illuminate language variation and use in the chosen San Francisco community.

courseDescr: A high-level introduction to the field of social psychology, with special attention to predominant theoretical and methodological themes, seminal research, contemporary advances, and Stanford contributions.
original_descr: A high-level introduction to the field of social psychology, with special attention to predominant theoretical and methodological themes, seminal research, contemporary advances, and Stanford contributions.
expanded_descr: Social Psychology offers a high‑level introduction to the discipline, guiding students through its core concepts and major areas of inquiry. Contemporary advances are examined to illustrate how the discipline evolves, and particular attention is given to notable contributions originating from Stanford. By integrating classic studies with recent findings, the class provides a comprehensive overview that prepares students to understand and critically evaluate social psychological phenomena in both historical and modern contexts.

courseTitle: Regression Models and Analysis of Variance
courseDescr: Modeling and interpretation of observational and experimental data using linear and nonlinear regression methods. Model building and selection methods. Multivariable analysis. Fixed and random effects models. Experimental design.
course_title: Regression Models and Analysis of Variance
original_descr: Modeling and interpretation of observational and experimental data using linear and nonlinear regression methods. Model building and selection methods. Multivariable analysis. Fixed and random effects models. Experimental design.

In addition, the course covers both fixed‑effects and random‑effects models, highlighting their distinct assumptions and applications. An integral component involves the principles of experimental design, enabling students to plan and evaluate experiments effectively. Throughout, emphasis is placed on practical implementation and critical assessment of regression and analysis‑of‑variance methods.

courseDescr: Weekly colloquia speaker series required for M.P.P. and M.A. in Public Policy students. Open only to Public Policy graduate students; permission number required to enroll.
original_descr: Weekly colloquia speaker series required for M.P.P. and M.A. in Public Policy students. Open only to Public Policy graduate students; permission number required to enroll.

This series provides a structured forum for engaging with invited speakers who address contemporary issues and research relevant to public policy, thereby supporting the academic development of all Public Policy graduate students.

courseTitle: Proseminar in East Asian Humanities I: Skills and Methods
courseDescr: Bibliographic, pedagogical, and research methods in East Asian Humanities.
course_title: Proseminar in East Asian Humanities I: Skills and Methods

By the end of the term, students will possess a solid methodological toolkit for advanced study and scholarly inquiry in East Asian Humanities.

courseDescr: Labor Seminar for Economics.

courseDescr: Restricted to Political Science Research Honors students who have completed POLISCI 299A.

courseDescr: Methods in Latin American Studies
original_descr: Methods in Latin American Studies

Through readings, discussions, and practical exercises, participants will deepen their methodological competence, preparing them for advanced inquiry within Latin American studies.

courseDescr: Microeconomic Theory Seminar (Only available for enrollment by ECON PhDs)
original_descr: Microeconomic Theory Seminar (Only available for enrollment by ECON PhDs)

original_descr: Open to Stegner Fellows in the Creative Writing Program only. May be repeated for credit.

courseDescr: For Ph.D. students in their first or second year who are or are about to be teaching assistants for the department. May be repeated for credit.
original_descr: For Ph.D. students in their first or second year who are or are about to be teaching assistants for the department. May be repeated for credit.

courseDescr: The elements of fiction writing: narration, description, and dialogue. Students write complete stories and participate in story workshops.
original_descr: The elements of fiction writing: narration, description, and dialogue. Students write complete stories and participate in story workshops.
expanded_descr: This course explores the fundamental elements of fiction writing, focusing on narration, description, and dialogue. Through a combination of instruction and practice, students will develop their ability to craft complete stories that integrate these core components effectively. The curriculum emphasizes hands‑on writing exercises, allowing each participant to produce full narratives that demonstrate mastery of narrative structure, vivid descriptive techniques, and authentic conversational exchange. In addition to independent writing, the class includes regular story workshops where students share their work, receive constructive feedback, and engage in collaborative discussions aimed at refining their craft. By the end of the term, students will have completed multiple stories and gained experience in peer review within a supportive workshop environment.

courseDescr: Conversation, grammar, reading, elementary composition. Daily sections may be set at the beginning of the quarter to suit schedule requirements.
original_descr: Conversation, grammar, reading, elementary composition. Daily sections may be set at the beginning of the quarter to suit schedule requirements.
expanded_descr: This first‑quarter, first‑year course introduces modern Chinese through a balanced focus on conversation, grammar, reading, and elementary composition. Students will engage in regular speaking practice to develop oral fluency, while systematic grammar instruction provides the structural foundation for accurate language use. Reading activities expose learners to authentic texts appropriate to their level, supporting vocabulary growth and comprehension skills. Elementary composition tasks enable students to produce simple written Chinese, reinforcing the integration of speaking, listening, reading, and writing. Daily sections are scheduled at the start of the quarter, allowing the instructor to arrange class times that meet the university’s scheduling requirements and accommodate student needs.

courseDescr: Identical particles; Fermi and Bose statistics. Time-independent perturbation theory. Fine structure, the Zeeman effect, and hyperfine splitting in the hydrogen atom. Time-dependent perturbation theory. Variational principle and WKB approximation.
original_descr: Identical particles; Fermi and Bose statistics. Time-independent perturbation theory. Fine structure, the Zeeman effect, and hyperfine splitting in the hydrogen atom. Time-dependent perturbation theory. Variational principle and WKB approximation.
expanded_descr: This course continues the study of quantum mechanics with a focus on systems of identical particles, exploring both Fermi‑Dirac and Bose‑Einstein statistics and their physical implications. It develops the formalism of time‑independent perturbation theory, applying it to fine‑structure corrections, the Zeeman effect, and hyperfine splitting in the hydrogen atom. The curriculum then introduces time‑dependent perturbation theory, emphasizing transition probabilities and interaction with external fields. Finally, the course covers the variational principle and the Wentzel‑Kramers‑Brillouin (WKB) approximation, providing tools for approximate solutions of quantum problems. Throughout, emphasis is placed on rigorous derivations and the underlying mathematical structure.

courseDescr: For students interested in research in political science, psychology, or communication. Methodological techniques for studying political attitudes and behaviors. May be repeated for credit.
original_descr: For students interested in research in political science, psychology, or communication. Methodological techniques for studying political attitudes and behaviors. May be repeated for credit.
expanded_descr: This graduate seminar offers an in‑depth exploration of methodological techniques used to investigate political attitudes and behaviors, making it ideal for students who are pursuing research interests in political science, psychology, or communication. The course emphasizes rigorous analytical tools and research designs that scholars can apply to their own projects, fostering a sophisticated understanding of how political phenomena are measured and interpreted. Participation is open to any graduate student whose academic focus aligns with these fields, and the seminar may be taken more than once for credit, allowing students to deepen their methodological expertise across multiple terms.

courseDescr: Required of all teaching assistants in Chemistry. Techniques of teaching chemistry by means of lectures and labs.
original_descr: Required of all teaching assistants in Chemistry. Techniques of teaching chemistry by means of lectures and labs.
expanded_descr: All teaching assistants assigned to the Chemistry department must complete this required course, “Teaching of Chemistry.” The program focuses on developing effective instructional techniques specifically for chemistry instruction, encompassing both lecture delivery and laboratory supervision. Participants will explore strategies for presenting complex chemical concepts clearly, managing classroom dynamics, and fostering student engagement during lectures. In the laboratory component, assistants will learn best practices for safety, equipment handling, and guiding students through experimental procedures. The course emphasizes practical, hands‑on experience that directly supports the dual responsibilities of teaching assistants in delivering high‑quality chemistry education across both lecture halls and lab settings.

courseDescr: Weekly lectures by experts from academia and industry in the field of chemical engineering. Course may be repeated for credit.
original_descr: Weekly lectures by experts from academia and industry in the field of chemical engineering. Course may be repeated for credit.
expanded_descr: The Colloquium provides a series of weekly lectures delivered by recognized experts drawn from both academia and industry, each focusing on current topics and developments within the discipline of chemical engineering. Participants attend these sessions to hear cutting‑edge research findings, emerging technologies, and professional perspectives that complement core coursework. The format emphasizes presentation and discussion, allowing students to engage with the material and ask questions of the speakers. Because the content varies with each offering, the course may be repeated for credit, enabling students to benefit from new lectures and insights in subsequent terms.

courseDescr: Theories of American politics, focusing on Congress, the presidency, the bureaucracy, and the courts.
original_descr: Theories of American politics, focusing on Congress, the presidency, the bureaucracy, and the courts.
expanded_descr: This course offers a comprehensive examination of the foundational theories that shape American politics, with particular attention to the nation’s principal institutions. Students will explore the structure, functions, and interrelationships of Congress, the presidency, the federal bureaucracy, and the judicial courts. Through critical analysis of classic and contemporary scholarly perspectives, the class investigates how these bodies operate within the constitutional framework, influence policy development, and interact with one another in the broader political system. Emphasis is placed on understanding the theoretical underpinnings that explain institutional behavior, power dynamics, and the role each entity plays in sustaining democratic governance in the United States.

courseDescr: An overview of the major forms of inequality in American society, their causes and consequences.  Special attention will devoted to to public policy associated with inequality.
original_descr: An overview of the major forms of inequality in American society, their causes and consequences.  Special attention will devoted to to public policy associated with inequality.
expanded_descr: This course offers a comprehensive overview of the major forms of inequality that shape American society, examining how disparities manifest across economic, racial, gender, and geographic dimensions. Students will explore the underlying causes of these inequities, including historical legacies, structural mechanisms, and contemporary social dynamics, and will analyze the wide‑ranging consequences for individuals, communities, and institutions. A particular focus will be placed on public policy, investigating how governmental actions, legislative frameworks, and policy interventions both respond to and influence patterns of inequality. Through critical discussion and analysis, the course aims to deepen understanding of the complex interplay between inequality and policy in the United States.

courseDescr: Focus is on improving grammatical accuracy and vocabulary, building fluency, and learning the structure and conventions of English correspondence, reports, and short academic papers. Enrollment limited to 14.
original_descr: Focus is on improving grammatical accuracy and vocabulary, building fluency, and learning the structure and conventions of English correspondence, reports, and short academic papers. Enrollment limited to 14.
expanded_descr: This course, titled Gateway to Graduate Writing, is designed to enhance students’ command of written English by concentrating on three core areas: grammatical accuracy, vocabulary development, and overall fluency. Participants will engage in targeted exercises that reinforce correct usage of grammar and expand lexical resources, while also practicing the organization and stylistic conventions typical of professional English correspondence, formal reports, and concise academic papers. Through repeated drafting, peer review, and instructor feedback, students will refine their ability to produce clear, well‑structured written work appropriate for graduate‑level communication. Enrollment is limited to fourteen students, ensuring a focused and supportive learning environment.

courseDescr: International Order and Disorder
original_descr: International Order and Disorder
expanded_descr: The course “International Order and Disorder” offers a focused examination of the forces that shape the stability and instability of the global system. It investigates the historical and contemporary patterns that contribute to the emergence of order among nations, as well as the conditions that give rise to disorder, conflict, and systemic disruption. Through critical analysis of case studies, theoretical frameworks, and empirical evidence, students will explore how political, economic, and social dynamics interact to produce both cooperative arrangements and periods of turmoil. The course emphasizes a nuanced understanding of the mechanisms that sustain international order and the challenges that threaten it, fostering a comprehensive grasp of global affairs.

courseDescr: (Formerly 279) Required of graduate students majoring in physical chemistry. May be repeated for credit.
original_descr: (Formerly 279) Required of graduate students majoring in physical chemistry. May be repeated for credit.
expanded_descr: Physical Chemistry Seminar (formerly numbered 279) is a required component of the graduate curriculum for students who have declared a major in physical chemistry. Participation in this seminar is mandatory for all such graduate students, ensuring that they engage with current topics, research discussions, and scholarly communication within the discipline. The course may be taken more than once, and each successful completion counts toward credit toward the graduate degree. No additional prerequisites, scheduling details, instructor information, or specific learning outcomes are introduced beyond the requirement that the student be a graduate major in physical chemistry and the allowance for repeat enrollment for credit.

courseDescr: Research on physics and mechanics of earthquakes, volcanoes, ice sheets, and glaciers. Emphasis is on developing theoretical understanding of processes governing natural phenomena.
original_descr: Research on physics and mechanics of earthquakes, volcanoes, ice sheets, and glaciers. Emphasis is on developing theoretical understanding of processes governing natural phenomena.
expanded_descr: This course offers an in‑depth exploration of the physics and mechanics underlying major geophysical phenomena, including earthquakes, volcanoes, ice sheets, and glaciers. Students will engage with current research literature and develop a solid theoretical framework for understanding the forces and processes that drive these natural events. Emphasis is placed on constructing and analyzing mathematical models that describe the behavior of the Earth's interior and surface systems. Through rigorous study, participants will gain a comprehensive grasp of the fundamental principles governing seismic activity, volcanic eruptions, and the dynamics of ice masses, preparing them for advanced inquiry in theoretical geophysics.

courseDescr: Intercultural Encounters in Korean Literature
original_descr: Intercultural Encounters in Korean Literature
expanded_descr: Intercultural Encounters in Korean Literature offers a focused exploration of the ways in which Korean literary works have engaged with, responded to, and been shaped by cultural exchanges throughout history. The course examines key texts and movements, highlighting how interactions with neighboring societies, trade routes, and global influences have left discernible marks on narrative forms, thematic concerns, and stylistic choices within Korean literature. Students will analyze representative examples to trace the dynamic dialogue between Korean authors and the broader cultural currents that have intersected with their creative output, gaining insight into the reciprocal nature of literary development across borders.

courseDescr: This class is open to graduate students in philosophy, all others need explicit permission. 2-unit option is only for Philosophy PhDs beyond the second year.
original_descr: This class is open to graduate students in philosophy, all others need explicit permission. 2-unit option is only for Philosophy PhDs beyond the second year.
expanded_descr: This graduate‑level seminar on Deflationary Theories of Truth is open to all philosophy graduate students. Students from other departments may enroll only if they obtain explicit permission from the instructor and department chair. The course is offered as a two‑unit option, but that credit level is restricted to Philosophy PhD candidates who have completed more than two years of their doctoral program. All participants must satisfy the prerequisite of graduate standing in philosophy, and any non‑philosophy graduate wishing to join must secure the required permission before registration. The class focuses on the central arguments and texts within deflationary accounts of truth.

courseDescr: Required of and limited to second year Mathematics graduate students.
original_descr: Required of and limited to second year Mathematics graduate students.
expanded_descr: This seminar is a required component of the graduate curriculum and is offered exclusively to students who are in their second year of the Mathematics graduate program. Enrollment is strictly limited to those individuals, ensuring that the class composition consists solely of second‑year Mathematics graduate students. No other students may register for the course, and participation is mandatory for all who meet this specific standing. The purpose of the seminar is to fulfill the program’s requirement for a graduate‑level teaching experience, and it is designed to be taken only by those who have successfully completed their first‑year coursework and are now advancing to the second‑year stage of their graduate studies.

courseTitle: RILE Colloquium on Race, Inequality, and Language in Education
courseDescr: This course is a workshop for PhD students focusing on interdisciplinary empirical work related to Race, Inequality, and Language in Education.
course_title: RILE Colloquium on Race, Inequality, and Language in Education
original_descr: This course is a workshop for PhD students focusing on interdisciplinary empirical work related to Race, Inequality, and Language in Education.
expanded_descr: This course is a workshop designed specifically for doctoral candidates who are engaged in interdisciplinary empirical research concerning race, inequality, and language within educational contexts. Participants will convene to discuss and develop scholarly projects that intersect these critical themes, drawing on methods and perspectives from multiple disciplines. The workshop format emphasizes collaborative inquiry, peer feedback, and the refinement of research designs that address how racial and socioeconomic disparities intersect with linguistic practices in schools and other learning environments. By the end of the term, PhD students will have advanced their understanding of these complex issues and strengthened the empirical foundations of their ongoing work.

courseTitle: Seminar in Music Perception and Cognition I
courseDescr: A seminar on topics in music perception and cognition. Students will study and discuss recent research as well as design and implement experiments.
course_title: Seminar in Music Perception and Cognition I
original_descr: A seminar on topics in music perception and cognition. Students will study and discuss recent research as well as design and implement experiments.
expanded_descr: This seminar explores current topics in music perception and cognition, inviting students to engage deeply with the field’s recent research literature. Through guided discussion and critical analysis, participants will examine key findings, theoretical frameworks, and methodological approaches that shape contemporary understanding of how humans perceive and process musical sounds. In addition to scholarly review, students will collaboratively design original experiments, formulate hypotheses, and develop appropriate experimental protocols. They will then implement these investigations, collecting and analyzing data to test their ideas. The course emphasizes both theoretical insight and practical research skills, fostering a comprehensive grasp of music perception and cognition while encouraging active, hands‑on inquiry.

courseDescr: Exploration of aspects of neurology, including subspecialties.  Current issues, clinical cases, and opportunities in the field.
original_descr: Exploration of aspects of neurology, including subspecialties.  Current issues, clinical cases, and opportunities in the field.
expanded_descr: This seminar offers an introductory exploration of neurology, guiding students through the breadth of the discipline and its various subspecialties. Participants will examine current issues shaping the field, engage with illustrative clinical cases, and discuss emerging opportunities for professional development and research. The course emphasizes a comprehensive overview, encouraging critical thinking about neurological practice while highlighting the interconnected nature of its sub‑areas. Through discussion and case‑based learning, students gain insight into contemporary challenges and potential career pathways within neurology, fostering a solid foundation for further study or specialization.

courseTitle: Lecture Seminar Series in Cancer Biology Program
courseDescr: Invited speakers share insights about state-of-the-art trends. Presents new concepts in the field of cancer biology. Science talks presented by students.
course_title: Lecture Seminar Series in Cancer Biology Program
original_descr: Invited speakers share insights about state-of-the-art trends. Presents new concepts in the field of cancer biology. Science talks presented by students.
expanded_descr: The Lecture Seminar Series in Cancer Biology Program offers a recurring forum in which invited speakers share their insights about current, state‑of‑the‑art trends shaping the discipline. Each session presents new concepts and emerging ideas that are advancing the field of cancer biology, providing participants with a timely overview of cutting‑edge research and theoretical developments. In addition to the expert talks, the series includes science presentations delivered by students, allowing them to showcase their own work and engage with the broader scholarly community. This format fosters a dynamic exchange of knowledge, encouraging both faculty and students to stay informed about the latest scientific progress in cancer biology.

courseDescr: Lorentz Invariance. S-Matrix. Quantization of scalar and Dirac fields. Feynman diagrams. Quantum electrodynamics. Elementary electrodynamic processes: Compton scattering; e+e- annihilation. Loop diagrams.
original_descr: Lorentz Invariance. S-Matrix. Quantization of scalar and Dirac fields. Feynman diagrams. Quantum electrodynamics. Elementary electrodynamic processes: Compton scattering; e+e- annihilation. Loop diagrams.
expanded_descr: This course introduces the fundamental concepts of quantum field theory, beginning with the principle of Lorentz invariance and its role in relativistic physics. It then develops the formalism of the S‑matrix, which encodes scattering amplitudes for particle interactions. Students will study the canonical quantization of both scalar fields and Dirac fields, establishing the groundwork for particle creation and annihilation operators. The curriculum includes a detailed treatment of Feynman diagrams as a graphical tool for calculating perturbative processes. Quantum electrodynamics is presented as a central example, and elementary electrodynamic processes such as Compton scattering and electron‑positron annihilation are examined in depth. The course also covers the construction and interpretation of loop diagrams within perturbation theory.
